content: 1. A dedicated educational session, such as a grand rounds or journal club, should be organized to focus on the management of traumatic brain injuries. This session should include detailed discussions on best practices and evidence-based approaches to improve outcomes in such cases. 2. A 20-year-old male involved in a motor vehicle crash was initially awake and alert but rapidly deteriorated due to profuse bleeding from a femoral artery laceration. He went into cardiac arrest during EMS transport and died shortly after arriving at the hospital. The autopsy revealed a large laceration of the right femoral artery and a right lung contusion. Deficiencies in hemorrhage control were identified, particularly in the prehospital setting, though documentation was insufficient to confirm this. Corrective actions include improving prehospital care systems, targeted education on hemorrhage control techniques, and better documentation practices. 3. A 20-year-old male pedestrian struck by a car initially felt only minor injuries and went home. Two days later, he became difficult to arouse and was brought to the hospital, where a CT scan revealed cerebral edema and subarachnoid hemorrhage. He was intubated after six hours in the ED and later developed hydrocephalus, requiring a ventriculostomy. He deteriorated and died one month after the injury. Deficiencies included delayed treatment of cerebral edema, delayed intubation, lack of follow-up CT scans, and poor documentation. Corrective actions include improving ED training, follow-up systems for discharged trauma patients, and documentation of vital signs. 4. A 16-year-old male motorcyclist was transferred from a private hospital to a trauma center without recorded vital signs. He was hypotensive upon arrival, underwent a negative laparotomy, and had orthopedic repairs for lower extremity fractures. He remained unstable and died 24 hours after arrival. The autopsy revealed a femur fracture, tibia fracture, right renal artery disruption, and retroperitoneal hematoma. Deficiencies included inadequate hemorrhage control, prolonged shock in the ED, and inappropriate definitive orthopedic repair in an unstable patient. Corrective actions include targeted education on managing shock, improved use of diagnostic tools like DPL or ultrasound, and enhanced communication between services. 5. A 75-year-old female with multiple medical problems sustained fractures of the radius, ulna, shoulder, and hip after a fall. She underwent five hours of orthopedic surgery on the night of admission despite being intermittently unstable. Postoperatively, she developed pneumonia and other complications, dying on postoperative day five. Deficiencies included inappropriate timing of surgery, lack of communication between services, and inadequate consideration of her instability and comorbidities. Corrective actions include policy changes requiring clearance from the primary service before surgery, targeted education on managing patients in shock, and reinforcing the concept of damage control surgery. 6. A 50-year-old male involved in a motor vehicle crash arrived at the ED with hypotension and a GCS of 5. He was intubated and received fluids and blood. A positive DPL was noted, but laparotomy was delayed for 11 hours, revealing 300 cc of blood and a pelvic hematoma. He developed multi-system organ failure and died on day 15. The autopsy revealed a pericardial effusion. Deficiencies included delayed bleeding control, insufficient attention to abdominal injuries, and unrecognized pericardial effusion. Corrective actions include improving ED staffing, targeted education on managing shock, and better utilization of trauma team resources. 7. A 68-year-old male with femur and pelvic fractures and facial lacerations arrived at the ED with respiratory distress and hypotension. He was intubated, but there was no documentation of repeat vital signs. He underwent plastic surgery for facial lacerations but did not receive fracture fixation. He died on day six. The autopsy revealed hydothorax and fractures. Deficiencies included inadequate fluid resuscitation, delays in fracture management, lack of leadership in resuscitation, and poor documentation. Corrective actions include improved ED staffing, better use of trauma teams, and targeted education on managing hemodynamically unstable patients. 8. A 60-year-old male involved in a motor vehicle crash arrived at the ED with hypotension and a positive DPL. He experienced cardiac arrest during evaluation and died despite CPR and thoracotomy. Autopsy revealed rib fractures, hemothorax, and liver lacerations. Deficiencies included delayed hemorrhage control, inadequate fluid resuscitation, and failure to follow ABCs in the face of unstable vital signs. Corrective actions include enhanced ED staffing, improved training for ED staff, and better documentation practices.
